name: Lake Merzbacher
full: Lake Merzbacher — an ice-dammed glacial lake on the Inylchek Glacier
near: Inylchek (Enylchek) — a half-abandoned settlement at the start of the valley, ≈40 km as the crow flies; Sary-Jaz — ≈38 km as the crow flies (OSM). The nearest inhabited points are the seasonal camps At-Jailoo (2500–2600 m) and Maida-Adyr (helipad), 30–40 km down the valley; ≈150 km by road to Karakol.
elev: 3304 m (MasterTour, ru-Wikipedia “3304 m a.s.l.”); the “Merzbacher meadow” camp is at 3400–3600 m (karakol.kg 3400, Ecotour/Horizon 3600); Advantour and Kyrgyzstan Travel give 3500 m — overstated compared with map data.
short: A “vanishing” lake between the North and South Inylchek glaciers, discovered by Gottfried Merzbacher in 1903: it fills with meltwater and once a year (usually in July–August) drains under the glacier within a few hours, causing a flood on the Inylchek and Sary-Jaz rivers. Access is only by a multi-day trek along the South Inylchek moraine from the border zone, or by helicopter flyover.
desc: Lake Merzbacher forms where the North Inylchek glacier butts against the South Inylchek: the glacier tongue blocks the valley, and meltwater accumulates behind the ice dam. The lower part (≈3.5–6 km long, ≈1 km wide) breaks through under the glacier every year, usually from mid-July to late August, and empties within hours to a day; the upper part, separated by an ice bridge, remains. The outburst raises the level of the Inylchek and Sary-Jaz rivers, which is why hydrologists monitor the lake. In 1903 the German geographer Gottfried Merzbacher saw the lake full on his way to Khan Tengri, and three days later empty, and the following year he confirmed that the phenomenon recurs regularly; the exact breakout mechanism is still debated. The lake lies in the border zone with China and Kazakhstan: a border service permit is required. The standard route: Karakol → Chon-Ashuu Pass (3822–3830 m) → Inylchek valley → At-Jailoo camp (2500–2600 m) → Iva camp (≈18 km) → Glina/Chon-Tash camp along the moraine → Merzbacher meadow (3400–3600 m) → side trip to the lake; ≈78–80 km over 5–6 days with climbs of up to 2000 m, walking on moraine and ice, river crossings and sections washed out by mudflows. Operators' seasonal camps run roughly from 5 July to 30 August. The alternative is a helicopter from Karkyra to South Inylchek with a flyover of the lake (Ak-Sai Travel), or combined programs with helicopter drop-off/pick-up.
guide: What is most interesting here is not the view but the timing: come in early July and you will see a turquoise lake with floating icebergs, in late August an empty basin with blocks of ice on the bottom, and both pictures are rare in their own way. At the Merzbacher meadow listen at night: the rumbling and cracking is the glacier “breathing”, and on the day of the outburst the glacier “comes alive with frightening sounds”, as the first eyewitnesses wrote. Set aside a spare day — weather and the state of the moraine dictate the schedule, and the camps work only in July–August. Arrange the border-zone permit at least a week ahead (through an operator, ≈3000 som in 2025) — without it you will be turned back at the second checkpoint in the valley. If you lack the legs or days, the helicopter tour from Karkyra shows both the lake and Khan Tengri in three days — expensive, but the only “quick” way.
see: The lower lake with icebergs (before the outburst) or its empty basin (after); the ice dam and the ice bridge between the upper and lower lake; the Merzbacher meadow; the South Inylchek glacier (≈60 km — one of the largest outside the polar regions) with multicolored glacial lakes along the way; views of Nansen Peak (5697 m), Khan Tengri (7010 m) and, in good visibility, Pobeda Peak (7439 m); a side trip to Panorama Peak (≈4500 m).
skip: If you don't have 6–13 free days, experience of high-altitude hikes and a budget from $1,500 — this is an expedition, not an excursion. If you are afraid of glaciers, crevasses and river crossings — the route goes over moraine and ice without a marked trail. If you want to be sure of seeing the “lake” — it may already be gone: the outburst happens as early as mid-July.
diff: Hard: 5–6 days of trekking over moraine and glacier, 78–80 km, total ascent ≈2000 m, elevations 2500–3600 m (4500 for Panorama Peak), river crossings, crevasses, sections washed out by mudflows; you need high-altitude hiking experience, good fitness and a guide. The alternative without trekking is a helicopter.
when: Late June to late August (operator camps: 5 July — 30 August). To catch the lake full — the first half of July; to see the empty basin — late August. In recent years the outburst has shifted to July, and sometimes there are two (July and late August). A winter outburst also exists, but access is closed in winter.
hours: Around the clock, but in practice only in the camps' working season (July–August) and with a border permit; the second border checkpoint is at the entrance to the Inylchek valley.
daytime: Morning — clear sky and views of Khan Tengri before the afternoon clouds; head out to the lake early so you can return to camp in daylight.
how: Only with a tour operator or your own logistics: Karakol → Inylchek village over Chon-Ashuu Pass (3822 m) by truck/4×4 → At-Jailoo camp (2500–2600 m; 1 day) → 3-day trek along South Inylchek to the Merzbacher meadow → side trip to the lake → 2 days back (or helicopter South Inylchek → Karkyra). Ak-Sai variant: Bishkek → Karkyra → helicopter to the Inylchek valley → trek to the meadow (day 6 of the program) → South Inylchek base camp → helicopter back. A border-zone permit is mandatory (takes ≈7 days to process).
needcar: Yes: a 4×4/truck drop-off from Karakol to At-Jailoo (≈150 km, 6–8 h) or a helicopter; beyond that, only on foot. Getting there on your own in a regular car is impossible.
self: Formally yes (with a permit and glacier-hiking experience), in practice most people go with an operator: the moraine route is not marked, the camps and food belong to the operators, and rescue is only through them. Asia Hikes describes an independent option with nights in camps for ≈$60/day.
roadtype: Karakol → Inylchek: paved to Ak-Suu/Ottuk, then a gravel mountain road over Chon-Ashuu Pass (3822–3830 m) and the Sary-Jaz valley — truck/4×4, 6–8 h; At-Jailoo → lake: a footpath along the lateral moraine and the ice of South Inylchek, river crossings, sections without a trail. There is no road access to the lake itself.
traveltime: Karakol → At-Jailoo ≈1 day by car; At-Jailoo → Iva camp ≈18 km (6–7 h) → Glina/Chon-Tash camp (3–5 h) → Merzbacher meadow ≈15 km (5–6 h) → lake and back (3–4 h); in total 78–80 km over 5–6 days of trekking. In the Ak-Sai program the lake is on day 6 of 13, allowing for the helicopter and acclimatization. The helicopter tour takes 3 days from Bishkek.
stay: Operators' tent camps: At-Jailoo (2500–2600 m), Iva, Glina/Chon-Tash (2900 m), Merzbacher meadow (3400–3600 m), South Inylchek base camp (4000 m); ≈$60/day with meals for independent travelers (Asia Hikes 2024), and Ak-Sai has permanent tents included in the tour. Before departure — guesthouses in Karakol or the Karkyra yurt camp.
net: There is no mobile signal in the Inylchek valley or on the glacier; operators have satellite phones/radios in the base camps. The last signal is at Karakol/Ak-Suu. There are no operator measurements; this comes from tour descriptions and trip reports.
entry: Khan Tengri Nature Park: 300 som per foreign tourist + 150 som per tent per night (Asia Hikes, updated 05.2024); with Ak-Sai the eco fees are included in the tour. Border permit: 3000 som/person via too.kg (2025, 50% prepayment, ≈7 days); Asia Hikes — $15–50 via operators. The park's official 2026 tariff was not found.
transfer: Trek with an operator: from $1,590/person (Ecotour, 6 days, 2025) to $3,200/person (Ak-Sai, 13 days with a helicopter, 2027); Ak-Sai helicopter tour — $1,050/person (3 days). A separate transfer Karakol → At-Jailoo by truck/4×4 is only on request from operators (Neofit, Karakol.kg); there is no public price list.
bring: Waterproof trekking boots, a sleeping bag rated to −5…−10 °C, a down jacket and warm layers, a rain jacket, poles, crampons/ice axe as required by the guide, sun protection (category 4 glasses, sunscreen), a first-aid kit with altitude sickness pills, a headlamp, a power bank, passport and permit, cash in som. The porter limit at Ak-Sai is 12 kg.
warn: It is a border zone — without a border service permit you will not be let in. At 3300–4000 m there is a risk of altitude sickness and you need to acclimatize. On the glacier: crevasses, moving moraines, river crossings; parts of the route are washed out by mudflows. On the day the lake breaks out the Inylchek and Sary-Jaz rivers rise sharply — do not pitch a camp by the water and follow your guide's instructions. The weather changes within an hour; snow in August is normal. Outside the camps there is no signal and no rescue infrastructure; insurance with helicopter evacuation is mandatory.
food: Only the operators' camp cooking (three meals a day are included in the tours, ≈$60/day for independent travelers): soups, porridges, tea; in Karkyra and Karakol before departure — kumys, boorsoks, beshbarmak. There are no cafes on the route.
reviews: Google Maps: 4.8/5, 19 ratings (03.10.2026). No TripAdvisor/2GIS cards. Trip reports (LiveJournal e_kaspersky, olly_ru; Skitalets) describe the lake as the main attraction of the trek to Inylchek; typical minuses are the hard moraine, the weather, and the cost of logistics.

p.sum: This is an expedition-level destination in the border zone: you cannot simply “drive” there on your own. The realistic options are (1) a 5–6 day trek from Karakol: a 4×4/truck over Chon-Ashuu Pass (5–6 h) to At-Jailoo camp, then 3 days along the South Inylchek moraine (≈78 km round trip) — with an operator from $1,590; (2) an Ak-Sai helicopter tour from Bishkek via the Karkyra base with a flyover of the lake (3 days, $1,050). Arrange the border permit 2–6 weeks ahead (too.kg 3000 som, 5–7 days); insurance with helicopter evacuation is mandatory. The window is mid-July to late August.

p.season: June — the approach is possible, but the camps are not yet working; 5 July — 30 August — camps and helicopters; first half of July — the lake is full, late July/August — an outburst is possible (the timing varies, and there can be two); September — cold, snow; October–May — closed.
p.budget.economy: ≈$1,000–1,500 for 6 days if organized independently: permit 3000 som, park fee 300 som + 150 per tent/night, transfer to At-Jailoo on request, camps $60/day
p.budget.comfort: $1,590 (6 days, Horizon/Ecotour) — $3,200 (13 days with a helicopter, Ak-Sai); helicopter tour $1,050
p.permits: 1) Border permit for the Inylchek/Khan Tengri zone (covers the Inylchek valley, Sary-Jaz, Khan Tengri base camp, Lake Merzbacher): via too.kg — 3000 som/person, 5–7 days (urgent 2–3 days for an extra fee), you need a passport scan, dates and route; the paper permit is collected at the Bishkek office (105/3 Isanov St) or delivered to Karakol; valid for 1 month. Other intermediaries — from $30/person, and they advise applying 2–6 weeks ahead in July–August. It is checked at the Maida-Adyr checkpoint and before boarding the helicopter at Karkyra. 2) Khan Tengri Nature Park: 300 som/foreigner + 150 som per tent per night + from 50 som per car (2024). 3) Insurance with helicopter evacuation.
p.access: Only for prepared trekkers with high-altitude hiking experience. Not for children, older people or wheelchairs; dogs are not advisable (glacier, border zone).
